source_text: Μηδεὶς ἐξαπατάτω ἑαυτόν; μήτε ὡς εὑρών, οὔτε γὰρ εὑρόντι κερδαίνειν ἔξεστι. Φησὶ γὰρ τὸ Δευτερονόμιον· Μὴ ἰδὼν τὸν μόσχον τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου καὶ τὸ πρόβατον πλανώμενα ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ ὑπερίδῃς αὐτά· ἀποστροφῇ ἀποστρέψεις αὐτὰ τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου. Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἐγγίζῃ ὁ ἀδελφός σου πρὸς σέ, μηδὲ ἐπίστασαι αὐτόν, συνάξεις αὐτὰ καὶ ἔσται μετὰ σοῦ, ἕως ἂν ἐκζητήσῃ αὐτὰ ὁ ἀδελφός σου καὶ ἀποδώσεις αὐτῷ. Καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις τὸν ὄνον αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀπώλειαν τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου, ὅσα ἂν ἀπόληται παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ, καὶ εὑρήσῃς αὐτὰ. Ταῦτα τὸ Δευτερονόμιον. Ἐν δὴ τῇ Ἐξόδῳ, οὐ μόνον ἐὰν τὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τις εὕρῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ· Ἀποστροφῇ, φησὶν, ἀποστρέψεις αὐτὰ εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ κυρίου αὐτῶν. Εἰ δὲ ἐν εἰρήνῃ ῥᾳθυμοῦντος καὶ τρυφῶντος καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ἀμελοῦντος ἀδελφοῦ ἢ ἐχθροῦ κερδάναι οὐκ ἔξεσται, πόσῳ μᾶλλον δυστυχοῦντος καὶ πολεμίους φεύγοντος καὶ κατὰ ἀνάγκην τὰ ἴδια ἐγκαταλείποντος;
thought_title: Restoring lost property as a sacred duty from Deuteronomy and Exodus
orientation: Gregory continues arguing that anyone who found and kept property from the devastated region has stolen from brothers, citing Deuteronomy's law on returning a brother's stray animals and Exodus's extension even to enemies' property.
pass_a_gloss: Let no one deceive himself; for neither is it permitted to a finder to gain. For Deuteronomy says: You shall not see your brother's calf and sheep wandering in the way and disregard them; by turning back you shall turn them back to your brother. But if your brother does not draw near to you, nor do you know him, you shall gather them and they shall be with you until your brother seeks them out and you shall restore them to him. And so you shall do with his donkey, and so you shall do with his garment, and so you shall do according to every loss of your brother, whatever he may have lost from him, and you shall find them. These things Deuteronomy. But in Exodus, not only if one finds the things of a brother, but also of an enemy; by turning back, it says, you shall turn them back to the house of their lord. If then in peace while a brother or enemy is living carelessly and luxuriating and neglecting his own things it is not permitted to gain, how much more when he is suffering misfortune and fleeing enemies and by necessity leaving behind his own things?

lemmas.gloss: to the one who finds, finder (dative singular)
by turning back, with a turning back (instrumental dative)
he seeks out, searches for thoroughly (aorist subjunctive)

choices.why: Imperative third person singular with reflexive; matches the pastoral warning tone.
Standard legal phrasing; ἔξεστι is impersonal with infinitive.

choices.english: by turning back you shall turn back
choices.why: Cognate accusative construction (dative noun + verb) preserved literally as in the LXX citation; conveys the emphatic restitution.
Two genitive participles describing the brother/enemy at ease; 'luxuriating' captures τρυφάω better than 'making merry'.

choices.english: by necessity leaving behind his own things
choices.why: κατὰ ἀνάγκην = under compulsion/necessity; ἐγκαταλείπω = leave behind, abandon.

bible_refs.note: LXX Deuteronomy 22:1-3: Μὴ ἰδὼν τὸν μόσχον τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου... ἀποστροφῇ ἀποστρέψεις αὐτὰ τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου... συνάξεις αὐτὰ... ἕως ἂν ἐκζητήσῃ αὐτὰ ὁ ἀδελφός σου καὶ ἀποδώσεις αὐτῷ· καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις τὸν ὄνον αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀπώλειαν τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου, ὅσα ἂν ἀπόληται παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ, καὶ εὑρήσῃς αὐτά.
LXX Exodus 23:4: Ἐὰν δὲ ἐν εἰρήνῃ... Ἀποστροφῇ ἀποστρέψεις αὐτὰ εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ κυρίου αὐτῶν. Gregory adapts the text: 'οὐ μόνον ἐὰν τὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τις εὕρῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ'.

pass_b_english: Let no one deceive himself; for it is not permitted to gain even if one finds something. Deuteronomy says: You must not disregard your brother's ox or sheep wandering on the road; by turning back you shall turn them back to your brother. If your brother is not near you and you do not know him, you shall gather them and they shall stay with you until your brother seeks them out and you shall restore them to him. You shall do the same with his donkey, and you shall do the same with his garment, and you shall do the same for every loss of your brother, whatever he may lose and you find. This is what Deuteronomy says. In Exodus, not only if one finds something of a brother but also of an enemy: by turning back you shall turn them back to the house of their master. If it is not permitted to gain from a brother or an enemy who in time of peace is living carelessly and luxuriating while neglecting his own things, how much more when he is suffering misfortune, fleeing enemies, and by necessity leaving behind his own things?

problems.quote: to the house of their Lord
problems.source_quote: εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ κυρίου αὐτῶν
problems.why: κύριος here means the animals' owner or master. A capitalized "Lord" makes readers think of God.
problems.fix: you shall turn them back to their owner's house.
problems.ruling: κυρίου αὐτῶν is their owner; capitalized Lord suggests God, misleading the Exodus reference.

problems.quote: who is living carelessly and luxuriating
problems.why: The English drops "in peace", which sets up the argument's contrast between peacetime and wartime flight.
problems.fix: from a brother or an enemy who in time of peace is living carelessly and luxuriating
problems.ruling: ἐν εἰρήνῃ omitted; peacetime contrast with fleeing enemies and necessity is weakened in the argument.

edits.old: you shall turn them back to the house of their Lord
edits.new: you shall turn them back to the house of their master

edits.old: from a brother or an enemy who is living carelessly and luxuriating while neglecting his own things
edits.new: from a brother or an enemy who in time of peace is living carelessly and luxuriating while neglecting his own things

fixed: "Lord" -> "master": τοῦ κυρίου αὐτῶν means the animals' owner, not God, so decapitalized.
Inserted "in time of peace" for ἐν εἰρήνῃ, restoring the peacetime contrast with wartime flight.
